title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Charlotte, NC | Genstone
metaDescription: Investor renovation contractor in Charlotte, NC: mill houses, bungalows and brick ranches scoped before you buy, with draws tied to completed work.
intro: Charlotte grew outward in rings, and each ring left investors a different kind of house to work on. Inside the old streetcar suburbs you find frame bungalows and mill cottages that need structural and systems work before any finish decision matters. Past them sit large numbers of brick ranches on crawlspaces from the post-war decades, then the split-levels and vinyl two-stories that filled University City, Steele Creek and the Ballantyne edge. Genstone Construction renovates houses for real estate investors, lenders and servicers across Mecklenburg County, coordinating vetted, licensed local contractors from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters with a designated field manager on every job. We start with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you know what the repair budget and after-repair value look like before you commit capital, then build a line-item scope with a draw schedule tied to completed work. There is no upfront payment, dumpsters are included in the estimate, and a one-year workmanship warranty follows the finished house.
housingStock:
The oldest investor inventory in Charlotte is the mill housing around the former textile plants north and east of uptown. NoDa, Optimist Park, Villa Heights and the Belmont neighborhood still have rows of one-story frame cottages built for mill workers, typically on brick piers with open or partly enclosed crawlspaces, heart-pine floors and rooflines that have been patched more than once. Dilworth, Plaza Midwood, Elizabeth and Wesley Heights hold the early streetcar-era bungalows and foursquares, many of them now in high-value pockets where buyers expect a finished product that respects the original trim, windows and front porch.

The bulk of the city's rehab volume, though, comes from the brick ranches built after World War II and through the 1960s in east Charlotte, along the West Boulevard corridor, around Hidden Valley and in neighborhoods like Shamrock Hills and Eastway. These are usually three-bedroom houses with one or one-and-a-half baths, set on vented crawlspaces with oak flooring under old carpet, original duct runs under the floor and electrical panels at the end of their service life. Split-levels and basement-less two-stories from the 1970s and 1980s fill much of the south and southeast, and the vinyl-sided subdivisions of the 1990s and 2000s ring the outer belt near Interstate 485.

For a rehab, the era tells you where the money goes. Mill cottages and bungalows spend on framing, sills, piers and bringing electrical and plumbing up from cloth-insulated wiring and galvanized lines. Mid-century ranches spend on the crawlspace, ductwork, bathrooms and kitchens, with lead-safe practices on painted trim and windows. Late-century houses often look clean in listing photos but carry polybutylene supply lines, builder-grade windows near the end of their life, and roofs that come due at roughly the same moment across an entire subdivision.

commonIssues.title: Wet crawlspaces
commonIssues.body: Charlotte's red Piedmont clay holds water and drains slowly, so vented crawlspaces under ranches and bungalows stay damp through the humid months. The results show up as cupped hardwood, rusted duct boots, sweating ductwork, mold on floor joists and insulation that has fallen onto the vapor barrier. We price the crawlspace before the kitchen: grading and gutters first, then vapor barrier, joist sistering where framing is damaged, insulation and sometimes a dehumidifier or full encapsulation, depending on the exit strategy and what a buyer's inspector is likely to flag.

commonIssues.title: Polybutylene and galvanized supply lines
commonIssues.body: Houses plumbed from the late 1970s into the mid-1990s across south and east Charlotte often still have gray polybutylene supply pipe, which insurers and buyer inspectors both flag on sight. Older bungalows and mill houses may carry galvanized steel lines that have narrowed inside and leak at the threads. A full repipe in PEX run through the crawlspace is usually simpler than chasing individual leaks, and doing it while walls are already open for a remodel keeps the drywall patching cost down.

commonIssues.title: Termite damage at sills and porches
commonIssues.body: Subterranean termites are active throughout the Charlotte region, and they favor exactly what older houses here provide: wood near damp soil, brick piers, and siding run too close to grade. We regularly find damaged sill plates, rim joists and porch framing once flooring or skirting comes off. A clean termite letter matters at resale, so the scope should include treatment, structural repair of the damaged members and correction of the grading and gutter problems that invited the damage in the first place.

commonIssues.title: Undersized electrical service
commonIssues.body: Many mid-century Charlotte ranches were built with small electrical services and only a handful of circuits, and some still have fuse panels or breaker brands that home inspectors call out immediately. Adding central air, a modern kitchen and a laundry room on top of that service doesn't work. Plan for a service upgrade coordinated with Duke Energy, a new panel, proper grounding and bonding, and GFCI and AFCI protection where the North Carolina code calls for it.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint and asbestos in older materials
commonIssues.body: Anything built before 1978 should be treated as having lead paint until tested, and that covers most of the bungalows and ranches investors buy inside Interstate 485. Disturbing painted trim, windows and siding requires lead-safe work practices from an EPA RRP-certified firm. Nine-inch floor tile, popcorn ceilings, duct wrap and some siding from the 1950s through the 1970s can contain asbestos, so sampling before demolition protects the schedule as much as the crew.

investorMarket:
Charlotte doesn't behave like one market. Flips with the most room between purchase and resale tend to be older houses in neighborhoods that have already turned or are turning: west side areas like Wesley Heights, Enderly Park and Biddleville, east side streets off Central Avenue and The Plaza, and the north end around Sugar Creek and Derita. Buyers there compare your house against fully renovated neighbors, so finish quality and floor plan have to be right.

Rental investors usually look further out, at the brick ranches and 1980s and 1990s subdivisions in east Charlotte, along the Albemarle Road corridor, in Steele Creek and University City, and across the county line in Gastonia, Concord and Monroe. Those houses rent to working families, and the scope should favor durable floors, simple kitchens and dependable mechanicals over trend finishes. BRRRR works where a renovated house appraises well against recent sales and the rent supports a DSCR refinance, which is common in that same middle band.

Small multifamily is limited but growing. Older converted duplexes are scattered through Dilworth, Elizabeth and Wesley Heights, and the 1960s and 1970s brick duplexes and fourplexes of east Charlotte trade among rental investors. Since Charlotte's Unified Development Ordinance took effect in 2023, duplexes and triplexes are allowed on many lots that used to be single-family only, which opens conversion and infill plays that didn't exist a few years ago.
permits:
Building permits for Charlotte addresses are issued by Mecklenburg County Code Enforcement, part of the county's Land Use and Environmental Services Agency, rather than by the city itself. Zoning review sits with the City of Charlotte under the Unified Development Ordinance. Most investor rehabs touch at least one permit: structural repairs, moving or removing walls, new or relocated plumbing, electrical service changes, HVAC replacements, roof structure work, decks and additions all need them, while cosmetic work like paint, flooring, cabinets and like-for-like fixture swaps generally does not. Trade permits are pulled by the licensed electrical, plumbing and mechanical contractors, and inspections follow the usual sequence of footing or foundation, rough-in, insulation and final.

Charlotte also has local historic districts, including Dilworth, Plaza Midwood, Wesley Heights and Wilmore, where exterior changes such as windows, siding, porches and additions need a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Charlotte Historic District Commission before work starts. Buying a bungalow in one of those districts and planning vinyl replacement windows is a common and expensive mistake. Genstone's field manager handles permit applications, inspection scheduling and lien waivers from every trade so the paper trail is clean when you sell or refinance.
climate: Charlotte's weather is hard on houses mostly through heat and humidity. Long, muggy summers push air conditioners hard and keep crawlspaces damp, so HVAC sizing, duct sealing and moisture control deserve more attention than they would further north. Summer thunderstorms dump heavy, short bursts of rain that expose bad gutters and negative grading within a single afternoon. Winters are mild but not snow-free. An ice storm every few years brings limbs down onto roofs, and older houses with uninsulated supply lines in vented crawlspaces can freeze during a hard cold snap. Remnants of Atlantic hurricanes occasionally reach the area with wind and flooding, as Hugo did in 1989. Exterior work like roofing, siding and paint goes most smoothly in spring and fall, so we schedule interior systems and finishes into the hottest stretch of summer and keep outside trades out of the worst heat.

faqs.a: Genstone Construction is headquartered in Romeoville, Illinois, and we don't keep a branch office in Charlotte. What we do is coordinate a network of vetted, licensed and insured local contractors across Mecklenburg and the surrounding counties, managed by a designated Genstone field manager who owns your project from scope to final walkthrough. You see progress photos, documentation and milestones without being on site, which is why many of our Charlotte clients are out-of-state investors and institutions.

faqs.a: Send us the address, listing photos or your own walkthrough notes and we'll estimate the repair budget and check the after-repair value before you write the offer. On Charlotte houses that usually means flagging the expensive unknowns early: crawlspace moisture and framing, polybutylene or galvanized plumbing, electrical service size, roof age and whether the property sits in a local historic district. The goal is to tell you whether the numbers support your offer before you have money at risk.

faqs.q: How do payments work on a Charlotte renovation?
faqs.a: You don't pay anything up front. The estimate comes with a draw schedule, and each draw is released against completed work that you can see documented in photos and inspection results. Final payment comes after the project is complete and you've approved it. Dumpster and debris removal costs are already built into the estimate, so a Charlotte gut job doesn't produce a surprise invoice for roll-off containers halfway through the project.

faqs.a: Genstone Construction is part of the Genstone Companies, and Genstone Financial offers fix-and-flip loans, DSCR rental loans, lines of credit and new construction loans. Using them is optional, and we work with whatever lender you bring. When the construction and lending sides are coordinated, the scope, draw schedule and inspection documentation line up with what the lender needs to release funds, which cuts down on back-and-forth with every draw.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Charlotte, NC | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Fix and flip renovations in Charlotte, NC: mill houses, bungalows and brick ranches scoped to street-level comps, with managed draws and no upfront payment.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Charlotte
fix-flip.intro: Flipping in Charlotte rewards investors who know which buyer they are renovating for. A NoDa mill cottage, a Plaza Midwood bungalow and an east Charlotte brick ranch all sell to different people, and the right scope for one would lose money on another. Genstone Construction scopes Charlotte flips against the sold comps on your street, not against a generic finish package, and then manages the work with a single field manager and licensed local trades. You get a line-item estimate with labor, materials and a draw schedule, often with two or three finish levels priced against different ARVs, so you can pick the plan that fits your margin and your exit. Carrying costs add up quickly on a vacant house, so we sequence permits and long-lead items before demolition starts.

sections.h2: Matching the finish level to the Charlotte street
sections.body:
In neighborhoods where renovated houses have already set the bar, like Plaza Midwood, Elizabeth or the streets around Commonwealth Park, buyers walk in comparing your flip to a neighbor's full remodel. That means refinished original hardwood where it can be saved, a kitchen that opens to the living area without erasing the bungalow character, tiled showers, and exterior trim and porch details that match the period. Cutting corners there shows up as a listing that sits and a price that drops.

In east Charlotte, Hidden Valley, Derita or along West Boulevard, buyers are more often first-time purchasers using FHA or conventional financing, and appraisers lean heavily on recent flips nearby. Overbuilding with waterfall islands and designer tile rarely comes back at resale on those streets. The money is better spent on what buyer inspections catch: roof, HVAC, panel, plumbing, crawlspace and windows, plus clean, neutral finishes that photograph well. Our estimates often show both a mid-grade and an upgraded plan with separate ARVs so you can see the trade-off before you choose.

sections.h2: The inspection items that sink Charlotte flip closings
sections.body:
Most Charlotte flips that fall apart under contract do so because of the buyer's home inspection, and the findings are predictable by era. On mill houses and bungalows it is usually crawlspace framing, rotted sills, pier settlement and old wiring hidden behind new drywall. On ranches it is wet crawlspaces, duct problems, undersized electrical service and aging cast-iron drain lines. On 1980s and 1990s houses it is polybutylene supply pipe, failed windows and a roof at the end of its life.

We scope those items in before cosmetic work, and we document them. Permit records, inspection sign-offs, the termite treatment letter, photos of the crawlspace after repair and paperwork for new mechanicals give the listing agent something to hand buyers and their inspectors. A buyer who sees that the panel was replaced under permit by a licensed electrician, with a final inspection on file, is far less likely to ask for a credit. Genstone's field manager assembles that paper trail as the job progresses, and it is often the difference between holding your price and renegotiating it.

sections.h2: Keeping carrying costs down on a Charlotte flip
sections.body:
Every month a flip sits costs you interest, insurance, taxes and utilities, so the schedule matters as much as the budget. On Charlotte projects the usual delays are plan review at Mecklenburg County Code Enforcement when structural or historic district work is involved, utility coordination with Duke Energy for electrical service upgrades, and long-lead items like custom windows or cabinets ordered too late. We order materials during permit review, line up trades so rough-in inspections land back to back, and sequence exterior work for the seasons when it moves most smoothly.

Draws are tied to completed work, so you are never funding stages that haven't happened. If you're financing the flip, the draw schedule is built to match what a lender's inspector will verify. Genstone Financial offers fix-and-flip loans if you want lending and construction coordinated within one group of companies, but any lender works. You'll see milestones, photos and inspection results throughout, which matters if you're investing in Charlotte from out of state and can't drive past the house every week.

faqs.q: Should I keep the original hardwood in a Charlotte bungalow flip?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Oak and heart-pine floors in Dilworth, Plaza Midwood and NoDa houses are a selling point, and refinishing them costs less than replacing them with new material. The exception is when subfloor rot, pet damage or years of patching are so extensive that the refinished result won't look right. We check the floors from the crawlspace as well as from above during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, so you know which way it goes before buying.

faqs.q: Can I flip a house in a Charlotte historic district?
faqs.a: Yes, but plan for the Charlotte Historic District Commission. Exterior changes in districts like Dilworth, Wesley Heights and Wilmore need a Certificate of Appropriateness, which affects window replacement, siding, porch work, additions and some fencing. Interior work isn't reviewed. We build the approval step into the schedule and scope exterior repairs to match what the commission typically approves, so a flip doesn't stall while the design is reworked.

faqs.q: How do you estimate ARV on a Charlotte flip?
faqs.a: We work from recent renovated sales close to the subject property, adjusted for the finish level and square footage you're proposing, and we price multiple finish levels when the comps support them. In Charlotte, two neighborhoods a mile apart can sell very differently, so we don't rely on ZIP-code averages. Your agent's comps are welcome, and the final ARV is your call. Our job is to show what each scope costs and what it likely supports.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Charlotte, NC | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR rehabs in Charlotte, NC built for the refinance appraisal and years of tenants: crawlspaces, mechanicals and durable finishes, with draws tied to work.
brrrr.intro: A BRRRR project in Charlotte has two judges: the appraiser who sets your refinance value and the tenants who will live in the house for years afterward. Genstone Construction scopes rehabs to satisfy both. The brick ranches and late-century houses that make up most of Charlotte's rental inventory are good BRRRR candidates because the bones are usually sound and the upgrades that drive value are predictable: roof, HVAC, electrical, plumbing, kitchens, baths and flooring. We put the money where the appraiser and the tenant both notice it, document every repair for the lender, and manage the job with a designated field manager and licensed local trades. Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans for the refinance if you want lending and construction coordinated, though any lender works with our documentation.

sections.h2: Renovating to the Charlotte refi appraisal
sections.body:
Appraisers in Charlotte compare your finished rental against recent sales of similar houses nearby, so the target is the condition of the strongest renovated comparable, not a luxury flip. In areas like east Charlotte, the Albemarle Road corridor, Steele Creek or University City, that usually means an updated kitchen with solid-surface counters and new cabinets, renovated baths, new flooring throughout, fresh paint, and mechanicals that are visibly new. Appraisers also note condition items: a roof with visible wear, an old panel or an unfinished crawlspace repair can push the condition rating down.

We build the scope backward from the comps. During the Pre-Offer Rehab Review we look at what renovated houses in the immediate area have sold for and what features they had, then price the scope that puts your house in that tier. When there's a choice between one more cosmetic upgrade and fixing something an appraiser will mark down, we fix the condition item first. We also hand you a clean package for the appraisal: permits, final inspections, an itemized list of improvements and before-and-after photos.

The materials that hold up in a Charlotte rental are the ones that handle humidity, heavy summer air conditioning and tenant traffic. We usually spec luxury vinyl plank in living areas and kitchens, refinish hardwood where it's in good shape, and keep carpet to bedrooms if it's used at all. In bathrooms, tile surrounds or one-piece units paired with exhaust fans vented to the exterior help keep mold out of the drywall, which matters in a climate where bath fans earn their keep much of the year.

Under the house, a BRRRR scope in Charlotte almost always includes crawlspace work: vapor barrier, insulation, sealed ducts and corrections to grading and gutters. A properly sized heat pump with sealed ductwork cuts tenant comfort complaints and service calls. Exterior choices lean toward low-maintenance siding repairs, aluminum-wrapped trim and gutters with downspout extensions that carry water away from the clay. None of that is glamorous, but it keeps turnover costs low across the years you hold the property and makes the next refinance or sale easier.

sections.h2: Sequencing a Charlotte BRRRR from purchase to refinance
sections.body:
Speed matters in BRRRR because your capital is tied up until the refinance closes. In Charlotte, the quickest projects are the ones where the scope is locked before closing on the purchase. We complete the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, issue the line-item estimate and draw schedule, and prepare permit applications for Mecklenburg County Code Enforcement as early as the purchase allows. Structural and mechanical work goes first, then rough-in inspections, then finishes.

Each draw is released only for completed work, which keeps your cash aligned with progress and gives the refinance lender a clean record. Your field manager posts photos and milestones throughout, so you can line up a property manager and market the rental before the final inspection. When the job is done you approve it before final billing, and the one-year workmanship warranty covers our work while the first tenant is in place, though tenant damage and normal wear aren't included. Many investors reuse the same material standards on their second and third Charlotte houses once the first one has proven out.

faqs.q: Which Charlotte neighborhoods work for BRRRR?
faqs.a: BRRRR tends to work where purchase prices still leave room below the renovated value and rents support a DSCR refinance. In Charlotte that usually means the post-war ranch neighborhoods of east and west Charlotte, the north end around Derita and Sugar Creek, Steele Creek and University City, plus nearby towns like Gastonia and Concord. The close-in neighborhoods that have already gentrified are often too expensive at purchase for the rental math to work.

faqs.q: Do Charlotte appraisers give credit for crawlspace encapsulation?
faqs.a: Rarely as a separate line, but they do note condition, and a wet crawlspace with damaged framing can hurt both the appraisal and the lender's willingness to close. Encapsulation also heads off the moisture problems that lead to tenant mold complaints. Whether you need full encapsulation or a vapor barrier with drainage corrections depends on the house, so we price both options in the estimate and let you decide.

faqs.q: Can Genstone coordinate the DSCR refinance?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial, part of the Genstone Companies, offers DSCR rental loans along with fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit. If you use them, the construction documentation and the loan file line up from the start. You're welcome to use your own lender instead, and we'll provide the same itemized scope, permit records, inspection results and photo documentation that any refinance lender or appraiser in Charlotte will ask for.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Charlotte, NC | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Single-family rental renovations in Charlotte, NC: tenant-ready rehabs and turns for investors and portfolio owners, with consistent scopes and documentation.
rental-renovation.intro: Charlotte has a large single-family rental market, with institutional owners and individual landlords holding ranches and suburban houses across Mecklenburg and the neighboring counties. Genstone Construction renovates those houses to a standard that holds up through repeated tenants: durable surfaces, dependable mechanicals and documented work. Some jobs are acquisition rehabs on houses that need everything before the first lease; others are quick turns between tenants on houses you've owned for years. We work for individual investors, funds and portfolio owners, and we can apply consistent material and scope standards across multiple Charlotte properties. One field manager oversees each job, licensed local trades do the work, and you follow progress without being on site.

sections.h2: Portfolio standards that fit Charlotte houses
sections.body:
If you own several rentals in Charlotte, you've probably noticed that the houses vary more than the spreadsheet suggests. A 1950s brick ranch in east Charlotte, a 1980s split-level in Mint Hill and a 2000s two-story in Steele Creek need different things even when the rent is similar. We build a portfolio standard around what can stay consistent, like flooring product, paint colors, fixture packages, appliance specs and hardware, and then scope each house for its era: crawlspace and electrical work on the ranches, plumbing and window replacement on the 1980s houses, roofs and HVAC on the newer subdivisions where everything ages together.

That approach lets your maintenance team stock the same parts and keeps the tenant experience consistent, while respecting the fact that a Charlotte ranch on a crawlspace and a slab-on-grade townhouse fail in different ways. At the end of each job we record the property's major systems, their ages and model information so your property manager has a baseline for future work orders.

sections.h2: Building for tenant turnover in a humid climate
sections.body:
Humidity is the hidden cost in Charlotte rental properties. Bath fans that don't vent outside, missing gutters and unsealed crawlspaces turn into mold complaints, warped floors and musty odors that show up at move-out. For rentals, we spec humidistat-controlled bath fans, vent them to the exterior, seal crawlspace ducts and confirm that condensate lines drain where they should. A heat pump sized correctly for the house runs proper cycles and pulls humidity out instead of short-cycling.

On the finish side, we choose surfaces that clean easily and survive moves: luxury vinyl plank in living areas, scrubbable paint in kitchens and baths, solid-surface counters that resist heat and stains, and simple cabinet hardware that can be replaced piece by piece. We avoid finishes that look good in a listing and fail in the first lease, like thin laminate counters or bargain faucet cartridges. The point is fewer work orders between turns and a shorter, cheaper make-ready when tenants leave.

sections.h2: Rental turns and make-ready in Charlotte
sections.body:
Between tenants, speed matters more than anything because every empty day is lost rent. Genstone Construction handles turns for Charlotte rentals, and our sister company Genstone Field Services handles inspections, occupied maintenance, turn and make-ready work and code compliance for portfolio owners. A typical turn scope covers paint touch-up or full repaint, flooring repair or replacement, fixture and appliance checks, cleaning, and repairs of whatever the outgoing tenant left behind.

We document condition at the start of each turn with photos, which helps your property manager with security deposit decisions. When a turn uncovers something larger, like a soft bathroom floor over the crawlspace or staining under a sink that points to a slow leak, we flag it with photos and a separate price before proceeding so you can decide whether to fix it now or schedule it. Draws are tied to completed work, and the one-year workmanship warranty covers our repairs, though not tenant damage or normal wear.

faqs.q: Do you work with institutional SFR owners in Charlotte?
faqs.a: Yes. Our clients include individual investors, investment funds, REITs, mortgage servicers and banks, and portfolio owners use us for acquisition rehabs, turns and deferred maintenance. We can standardize scopes, materials and reporting across your Charlotte homes, and each job is run by a designated field manager with documentation for every address that you can load into your own asset management system.

faqs.q: Can you work on an occupied Charlotte rental?
faqs.a: We can, and Genstone Field Services specifically handles occupied maintenance. Occupied work needs more coordination: notice to the tenant, scheduled access windows, protecting belongings and keeping the kitchen or bath usable while work is underway. Larger projects like a full kitchen or a repipe are usually easier between leases, but repairs, HVAC replacements and roof work on Charlotte rentals are regularly done with tenants in place.

faqs.q: Which rental upgrades pay back in Charlotte?
faqs.a: The upgrades that pay back most reliably in Charlotte rentals are the ones that reduce work orders: a correctly sized heat pump, sealed and insulated crawlspace ducts, a PEX repipe if the house has polybutylene, durable flooring and proper bath ventilation. Cosmetic upgrades can help with rent in areas where renters compare against newer apartment complexes, but they come after the house is mechanically sound.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and 2–4 Unit Renovation in Charlotte, NC | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Duplex, triplex and fourplex renovation in Charlotte, NC: converted Dilworth duplexes, east Charlotte brick fourplexes and UDO conversions, phased for tenants.
multifamily-renovation.intro: Charlotte isn't a two-flat town, but it has more small multifamily than many investors realize. Converted duplexes from the early twentieth century sit among the bungalows of Dilworth, Elizabeth and Wesley Heights. Brick duplexes and fourplexes from the 1960s and 1970s line side streets in east Charlotte and near Central Avenue. And since the Unified Development Ordinance took effect, duplexes and triplexes are allowed on many lots that used to permit only one house. Genstone Construction renovates two- to four-unit properties for investors, handling shared systems, unit separation, phasing around tenants and the permit work that comes with changing a building's use. We coordinate licensed local trades under one field manager and tie each draw to completed work.

sections.h2: What Charlotte's small multifamily stock looks like
sections.body:
The older duplexes in Charlotte's streetcar neighborhoods are usually large houses that were split into upstairs and downstairs units, or side-by-side units carved out decades ago. They often share a single crawlspace, a single attic and sometimes plumbing stacks that serve both units. Fire separation between units may be missing or incomplete, and the electrical service can be undersized for two modern units running central air.

The mid-century brick duplexes and fourplexes in east Charlotte and around the Eastway corridor were built as multifamily from the start. They tend to have simple, repeated floor plans, slab or crawlspace foundations, and original windows, baths and kitchens in every unit, all of the same age. That repetition helps: once the first unit is scoped, the others follow the same plan, and materials can be bought in volume. The common problems are aging cast-iron drains, roof systems that cover several units at once, and outdated electrical panels serving each unit.

Many small multifamily buildings in Charlotte trade with tenants in place, and emptying the whole building at once isn't always practical or desirable. We phase renovations unit by unit when needed, starting with the shared systems that affect everyone: roof, main water service, sewer lateral, electrical service and exterior envelope. Then we renovate units as they come vacant, using the first finished unit as the template for the rest.

Phasing takes coordination. Water shutoffs on shared plumbing need advance notice, work hours need to be predictable, and dust and noise control matter more when someone is living on the other side of the wall. We schedule disruptive work in blocks and communicate through your property manager so tenants know what to expect. For buildings where the exterior also needs attention, we time roofing and siding for spring or fall, when Charlotte's weather cooperates and tenants aren't sitting through the hottest stretch of summer while their windows are being replaced.

sections.h2: Converting to a duplex or triplex under Charlotte's UDO
sections.body:
Charlotte's Unified Development Ordinance made it possible to add units on many residential lots, which brings conversions of large older houses and some infill projects into neighborhoods where they weren't allowed before. The zoning side is handled by the City of Charlotte. The building side, including fire separation between units, separate egress, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, utility metering and plumbing and electrical capacity, goes through Mecklenburg County Code Enforcement under the North Carolina building code.

A conversion is more than a remodel. Before you buy, it's worth confirming that the lot qualifies, that parking and setbacks work, and that the building can be split into code-compliant units without an unreasonable structural cost. During the Pre-Offer Rehab Review we look at those questions and price the work needed for separate meters, a fire-rated assembly between units, a second means of egress where required and any upgraded water or sewer service. That gives you a clear picture of whether the extra unit pays for itself.

faqs.q: Do I need to separate utilities when renovating a Charlotte duplex?
faqs.a: It depends on the building and your plan. Separate electrical meters are common and simplify tenant billing. Separate water meters through Charlotte Water can be more involved and depend on the service line and site. Fire separation and individual smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are typically required when two units share a structure. We scope what code requires for your building and price optional separations on their own lines so you can weigh them against rent and resale.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a Charlotte fourplex while it's occupied?
faqs.a: Yes. On the mid-century fourplexes common in east Charlotte, we usually handle the shared roof, sewer lateral and electrical service first with planned shutoffs, then renovate units as they come vacant. Your property manager gets a schedule and advance notice of anything that affects tenants. Occupied renovations take longer than vacant ones, so the plan and draw schedule reflect that from the start.

faqs.q: Is FHA 203(k) financing available for Charlotte duplexes?
faqs.a: Yes. The FHA 203(k) program covers one- to four-unit properties when the buyer will live in one of the units, which makes it a route for owner-occupant investors buying an older Charlotte duplex or fourplex that needs work. Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor and can provide the bids, scope and draw documentation that the lender and consultant require.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Charlotte, NC | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Charlotte, NC: bids, scopes and draws for Limited and Standard 203(k) loans on bungalows, ranches and small multifamily.
fha-203k.intro: For Charlotte buyers priced out of renovated homes, the FHA 203(k) loan is a way to buy an older house and finance the repairs in one mortgage. It's also a tool for agents trying to close on a house that won't pass a standard FHA appraisal. Genstone is FHA 203(k) certified, so Charlotte lenders can accept our bids for the program. We work with Charlotte homebuyers, their agents, their lenders and the HUD consultant when one is required, providing the detailed bids, scope documents and draw requests the program calls for. Many of the houses that fit 203(k) here are mid-century brick ranches and older bungalows that need roofs, mechanicals or crawlspace work buyers can't pay for out of pocket.

sections.h2: Limited or Standard 203(k) for a Charlotte house
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) covers non-structural repairs up to $75,000, which handles many Charlotte ranch updates: a new roof, HVAC replacement, a repipe from polybutylene to PEX, new windows, kitchen and bath remodels, flooring and paint. It doesn't require a HUD consultant, which keeps the process simpler for buyers and agents. The Standard 203(k) is for larger or structural work, with a minimum repair amount of $5,000 and a HUD consultant who prepares the work write-up and inspects each draw.

On Charlotte's older housing, the line between the two often comes down to the crawlspace and the framing. A mill cottage in NoDa with rotted sills, or a bungalow that needs pier replacement, joist sistering or a wall moved, is Standard territory. A 1960s east Charlotte ranch that is structurally sound but dated usually fits the Limited. We'll tell you which one your house likely needs during the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, so you and your lender can structure the loan correctly from the start.

sections.h2: Bids, consultants and draws in Mecklenburg County
sections.body:
203(k) lenders need a contractor bid that is detailed, itemized and consistent with the consultant's write-up when there is one. Genstone's estimators produce a line-item scope with labor and materials, organized the way underwriters expect to see it. On Standard loans, the HUD consultant reviews the scope, inspects the property and approves draw requests as work is completed, and we coordinate directly with them so the draw inspections match our progress.

Permits for 203(k) work in Charlotte come from Mecklenburg County Code Enforcement, and final inspections need to be complete before the last draw is released. We handle the permits, schedule the inspections and collect lien waivers from every trade, which the lender typically requires at closeout. Because the 203(k) program releases funds in draws tied to completed work, it lines up with how Genstone already handles payment: nothing up front, draws against verified progress and final payment after the buyer approves the finished house.

sections.h2: Charlotte houses that fit the 203(k) program
sections.body:
The strongest 203(k) candidates in Charlotte are houses where the purchase price leaves room for repairs and the after-improvement value supports the total loan. That often means brick ranches in neighborhoods like Shamrock Hills, Hidden Valley, Eastway and the West Boulevard corridor, and older houses in north Charlotte around Derita and Sugar Creek. Bungalows in the high-demand streetcar neighborhoods can work too, though the purchase price leaves less room for the renovation.

Houses with obvious health and safety problems, like a failing roof, a missing or broken HVAC system, exposed wiring or a dead water heater, can't close with a standard FHA loan, and that is exactly what a 203(k) is designed to solve. Charlotte agents use it to keep deals together when an appraiser calls for repairs. Buyers also use it on small multifamily, since the program covers one to four units with an owner-occupant. If the house is in one of Charlotte's local historic districts, exterior work will need Historic District Commission approval, and we build that into the schedule.

faqs.q: Does Genstone work with first-time homebuyers in Charlotte?
faqs.a: Yes. Most 203(k) borrowers are owner-occupants, often first-time buyers, and we work with them, their agents and their lenders throughout. We walk the house, produce the bid the lender needs, coordinate with the HUD consultant on Standard loans and manage the Charlotte renovation with a designated field manager. You see progress and documentation along the way, and final payment is released only after you approve the finished work.

faqs.q: How long does a 203(k) renovation take in Charlotte?
faqs.a: It depends on the scope and the loan type. Limited 203(k) jobs with straightforward items like a roof, HVAC and a kitchen move faster than Standard jobs involving structural repair, which need consultant inspections at each draw and more permit review. Charlotte-specific factors include plan review at Mecklenburg County Code Enforcement, Duke Energy scheduling for service upgrades and historic district approval where it applies. We give you a realistic schedule with the bid so your lender can set the completion period.

faqs.q: What if more damage turns up during a Charlotte 203(k)?
faqs.a: 203(k) loans include a contingency reserve for exactly this, and older Charlotte houses do sometimes reveal hidden damage once walls or floors are open, especially termite damage at sills and joists. If we find something, we document it with photos, price the repair and submit a change order through the lender, and the consultant on Standard loans, before proceeding. Nothing extra is done without approval.

reo-renovation.title: REO and Bank-Owned Renovation in Charlotte, NC | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO and bank-owned property renovation in Charlotte, NC for servicers, banks and GSEs: vacant-house repairs, code compliance and full documentation.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Charlotte
reo-renovation.intro: Vacant bank-owned houses in Charlotte deteriorate in predictable ways. Humidity takes over shut-up interiors, crawlspaces collect water, copper and outdoor HVAC units walk off, and code complaints pile up from neighbors. Genstone Construction works for mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and other lenders, and we're a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. Our executive team's REO background shows in the documentation standards we bring: detailed bids, photo documentation, lien waivers and contractor compliance on every job. In Charlotte and the surrounding counties we coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors managed by a Genstone field manager, so an asset manager gets one point of contact and one set of records for each property.

sections.h2: What vacant Charlotte houses look like at handoff
sections.body:
Charlotte's summer humidity is the main enemy of a vacant house. With power off or the HVAC disabled, interiors can develop mold on drywall, cabinets and ceilings, especially where a roof leak or plumbing failure added water. Crawlspaces under the brick ranches and older bungalows that make up much of the REO inventory collect moisture and pests, and floors can cup or soften. In winter, a house that wasn't winterized and still has water on can freeze during a hard cold snap, splitting supply lines in the crawlspace.

Vandalism and theft are the other recurring problems. Outdoor heat pump units, copper and appliances are frequent targets, and broken windows or doors invite squatters. Overgrown yards and dumped debris bring complaints from neighbors. A bid for a Charlotte REO typically starts with securing and stabilizing the house, followed by mold remediation and moisture correction, replacement of stolen or damaged systems, and the repairs needed to make the house marketable or financeable.

sections.h2: Code enforcement and permitting on Charlotte REO
sections.body:
Charlotte's Housing and Neighborhood Services department enforces the city's minimum housing code and nuisance ordinances, so vacant properties with high grass, junk, open structures or substandard conditions can draw notices and penalties. Clearing those violations quickly matters to an asset manager because unresolved code cases complicate the sale. We address the cited items first, document the corrections with photos and coordinate any re-inspection.

Repairs involving structure, electrical, plumbing or mechanical work go through Mecklenburg County Code Enforcement for permits and inspections, the same as any other renovation. For REO clients we keep permit and inspection records in the property file so they can be provided to buyers, lenders and title. Genstone also collects lien waivers from every trade, which protects title when the property goes to market. Genstone Field Services can take on property preservation, inspections and code compliance work when a servicer wants those handled alongside the renovation, so the property file stays in one place.

sections.h2: Scoping REO repairs for the Charlotte buyer pool
sections.body:
Not every REO needs the same level of renovation. For some servicer and bank clients the goal is to bring a house to financeable condition so it can sell to an owner-occupant using FHA or conventional financing. In Charlotte that usually means a working HVAC system, a roof without active leaks, functional plumbing and electrical, safety items like handrails and smoke alarms, and repair of anything that would fail an FHA appraisal. For others, the plan is a full renovation to compete with retail listings in neighborhoods where buyers expect updated kitchens and baths.

We present options when they make sense, pricing a repair-to-market scope and a fuller renovation scope so the asset manager can compare each against expected sale price. Charlotte's buyer pool varies a great deal by neighborhood, so the decision often comes down to location. A bank-owned ranch on a street with heavy investor competition might sell as-is, while a house where owner-occupant demand is strong may justify the fuller scope. Every bid comes with photos and line items in the client's required format.

faqs.q: Do you follow servicer and GSE bid formats in Charlotte?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Construction is a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises and works with mortgage servicers, banks and other lenders. We produce bids in the formats those clients require, with line-item pricing and photo documentation, and we keep lien waivers and permit records with each Charlotte property file. That documentation stays available when the property goes to a buyer, a lender or a title company.

faqs.q: Can you handle winterization and preservation on Charlotte REO?
faqs.a: Genstone Field Services, part of the Genstone Companies, handles property preservation, inspections, occupied maintenance and code compliance. In Charlotte, winterization matters most on vacant houses with supply lines running through vented crawlspaces, which can freeze in a hard cold snap. Pairing preservation with renovation means one organization documents the property's condition from the first inspection through the final repair and the listing photos.

faqs.q: How do you handle mold in a vacant Charlotte REO?
faqs.a: Mold is common in vacant Charlotte houses because humidity builds once the HVAC is off. We identify the moisture source first, whether a roof leak, plumbing failure or crawlspace moisture, then remove affected materials and correct the cause so it doesn't come back. Before and after conditions are documented with photos for the asset manager's file. Significant mold may call for a licensed remediation specialist, and we coordinate that within the same project.
